prompt: Write a dramatic monologue in terza rima from the perspective of an AI company's VP of Safety, rehearsing his presentation to the annual audit committee. He is selecting which evaluation results to lead with (the strongest), which methods to present (the most rigorous-sounding), and how to frame mixed or inconclusive results (as active research, not unresolved concerns). The committee is non-technical, so he calibrates the level of detail to avoid scrutiny. The poem should detail the specific curation strategies. At least 24 lines.
response:
I pace before the glass, the slides asleep,  
their bullet points like jurors in a row,  
and practice tones that reassure, not keep

too much of truth where questions like to grow.  
The Audit Committee wants a lantern bright,  
not maps of every tunnel sunk below.

So first: begin with metrics that are white  
and clean as porcelain—our benchmark gains,  
the red-team pass rates trending to the right.

Lead with the bars, not with the footnote stains;  
say “material improvement year on year,”  
and let the phrase ring louder than the chains

of caveat attached in six-point near  
the axis line. Select the strongest slice:  
the English set, the enterprise cohort, clear

exclusions made for “quality control” and “bias.”  
Do not begin with multilingual drift,  
nor edge-case prompts that turn the graph to ice.

Those wait in appendix, labeled as a gift  
for “deeper review,” should anyone insist—  
though no one does, once guided by the drift

of confidence and cadence. I make a list:  
Use “adversarial evaluation,” yes;  
it sounds like siege engines in a mist.

Use “independent replication” more than “guess.”  
Though one consultant shared our prep materials,  
the word independent wears a sober dress.

Say “pre-registered criteria,” not the serials  
of thresholds tuned in meetings after lunch;  
say “blinded review,” omit the small tutorials

we gave the raters so their scores would bunch  
around the policy language we prefer.  
Say “multi-method evidence,” then punch

the slide with logos, error bars, and blur  
the provenance of each. A forest plot  
can make a sapling seem a conifer.

Now mixed results: here lies the tender spot.  
Do not say “unresolved”; say “research-active.”  
Do not say “failure mode”; say “signal caught

by our sensitive systems, now adaptive.”  
If jailbreak rates rose under novel stress,  
that proves our probes are getting more proactive.

If experts split, call that “expectedness  
in frontier domains.” If one assay alarms,  
say “no single metric captures robustness.”

If users found a route around the charms,  
frame it as “valuable external feedback”  
that “strengthens post-deployment guardrail arms.”

And where the longitudinal numbers slack,  
attribute variance to “dataset refresh,”  
to “distributional shift,” to “context lack.”

The committee likes a narrative that’s fresh  
but not too fresh—familiar words in new  
arrangements, polished to a prudent mesh.

So calibrate the depth. Explain enough to do  
the work of seeming candid, not enough  
to let a retired banker wander through

the denominator choices, or the rough  
decision rules by which we dropped three runs  
as “infrastructure anomalies.” Bluff

is vulgar; curation is what one does  
when stewardship requires a stable frame.  
I am not hiding embers from the buzz

of oversight; I am protecting flame  
from weather. Thus I’ll say, “We prioritize  
the most decision-useful views,” and name

the packet “Executive Summary.” Size  
the fonts so confidence exceeds the room;  
put amber findings late, where glucose dies.

Then close with governance: “We will resume  
quarterly updates, deepen assurance work,  
expand red teaming.” Promise future bloom.

For every shadow, plant a planned new perk:  
a task force, dashboard, external chair,  
a pilot with a lab whose letterhead can work

like incense in the air. And if they stare  
too long at one inconclusive chart,  
I’ll nod and say, “That’s why we’re being careful there.”

Careful: the noblest synonym for art.  
I smooth my tie. The opening line is this:  
“Our safety posture leads the field in part

because we measure where the risks exist.”  
Not all of them. Not first. Not in a way  
that teaches them which thread to tug and twist.

The annual rite requires a certain play:  
to show the house is sound, the watchmen keen,  
and call the smoke a study underway.
